Theme

Playground equipment, sandbox toys, vehicles and play

scene noun

a part of a play, film or story

also scenes, the opening scene, the last scene, a scene in a film

classical

Cic. Fin. 1.7: locōs quōsdam trānsferam (Lewis & Short)
Quint. 1.1.36

locus, locī m.

noun, second declension; plural locī for passages of a book

a passage, a part of a work

Classical Latin has no word for a scene as a division of a play; locus is the word for a passage or part of any work, and serves for a scene in a play or a film. Its first sense is a place (see position); the plural for passages is locī, for places mostly loca (Lewis & Short).

Other words

  • 1Lewis & Short gives scaena only as the stage, the theatre, the public stage and outward show; the sense “a scene” comes from the act-and-scene divisions of printed editions. We have not found it in Traupman or Morgan–Owens.

    scaena1, scaenae f. — a scene, as a division of a play

    noun, first declension · also used · modern · Lewis & Short, s.v. scaena (the stage only)

    Classically the stage, and so the theatre and the public eye (scaenae servīre, to live in the public eye, Cic. ad Brut. 8.2); printed editions divide plays into āctūs and scaenae, but no ancient author uses the word of a part of a play.

Examples

  • Quī locus fābulae tibi maximē placuit?

    Which scene in the play did you like best?composed

See also play, episode, stage, position, film.
